messages.author: 4a5714f5e55ca8cf
messages.subject: Help with Zig-Zag Survey Designs
parts:
Hi,=20=20

I'm new to Program Distance and looking for some advice. We are surveyin=
g=20
eider ducks on the northern edge of their wintering range in eastern Cana=
da.=20=20
We are using a survey design described by D. Bordage et al. (1998; JWM=20=

62:185=96192). The survey is timed with maximum ice coverage. At this t=
ime=20
flocks can be very large and thieir distribution is very restricted. Bef=
ore=20
conducting the survey we monitor the daily ice cover maps to ensure we=20=

cover all areas that have open water. Daniel did some work with double=20=

counts of small flocks (<80). He found there was a very high detection r=
ate=20
for small flocks, and more importantly, only a small proportion of the po=
pulation=20
occurred in small flocks. He found most of variance in the estimates was=

due=20
to observer error in flock estimates for large flocks.

We felt we had a good survey design for the environment we're working in.=
=20=20
However, we know there are some sources of variance that we do not=20

account for. Mostly I'm thinking about how flock sizes and their geograp=
hic=20
distribuiton may vary with ice (low) cover.=20=20

In the past I stratified the coast into areas with high and low potential=
for=20
wintering eiders. We completly cover all the high strata using photo cor=
rected=20
counts. For the low strata. I would like to sample segments of the low s=
trata=20
using zig-zag distance survey. This would at least allow us to assess th=
e=20
importance of the low strata -- I'm not sure if I'm explaining my self we=
ll.

Before I heard of Distance, I created a grid of 0.1 by 0.1 degree and ass=
igned=20
each grid cell to high or low strata the calculated total the number of c=
ells in=20
each strata. I set the sampling intensity at 20% and the sampling unit a=
t 3=20
grid (adjacent) cells (a rectangle of about 20*30 km), and selected rando=
m=20
start points. What I'd like to do with Distance is use the same idea and=
use=20

random start points for ZIG-ZAG surveys (maybe covering 30 km of linear=20=

coastline) to sample the low strata.=20=20

Finally my questions:=20=20

1) The coastline has some complex shapes, and I undestand that the Zig-Za=
g=20
design can result in uneven probability of coverage in these situations. =
To=20
simplify the design I was thinking about making retangular sampling areas=
set=20
at the randon start points (say 30 * 5 km), aligning the long axes with t=
he=20
coastline and insetting the rectangle into the coastline slightly. This =
would=20
result in some transects having the vertices cut off where they overlap w=

ith=20
the land - does this sound reasonable.
2) I would like to have some general comments/critisim of the general sur=

vey=20
design.

Thanks
Scott Gilliland
Canadian Wildife Service
6 Bruce St.=20
Mount Pearl, NL
A1N 4T3

--

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Help with Zig-Zag Survey Designs
parts:
Scott:

You have a lot of issues that you touch upon in this note, cluster size=20
variability being a considerable matter. But to move directly to the=20
points that are of greatest interest to you, I direct you to a recent=20
publication by my colleague Len Thomas and co-authors

Thomas, L., R. Williams and D. Sandilands. 2007. Designing line transect=20
surveys for complex survey regions. Journal of Cetacean Research and=20
Management 9: 1-13.

You can download the paper and also some of the Distance projects used=20
in that survey (of complex coastline of British Columbia) from Len's=20
website:
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/pubs.html

The paper goes into considerable detail discussing coverage probability=20
from zigzag designs, and the manner in which a study region can be=20
broken into substrata to address the coverage issue (as well as reduce=20
the amount of off-effort flight time).
